title: Railways: the Bharatiya Railway Mazdoor Sangh
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Railway workers, secret-ballot recognition and BRMS: how the December 2024 ballot went, what the 1974 strike showed, and the issues railway unions raise.
body:
Indian Railways is a workplace, a public service and a piece of national history all at once. Its employees run the trains, maintain the track, repair coaches in workshops, sell tickets and keep signals working. The **Bharatiya Railway Mazdoor Sangh (BRMS)**, listed on the BMS website as the Bharatiya Railway Mazdoor Mahasangh, is the BMS-affiliated federation among them. This post looks at where the railway workforce has come from, how unions win recognition, what BRMS's position is and what railway employees' demands look like in practice.

## A long labour history

Railway workers have been at the centre of Indian labour history for as long as there have been railways. Wikipedia notes that the earliest recorded railway strike in India took place in Howrah in 1862, and that there were strikes in 1967, 1968, 1970 and 1973 before the great strike of 1974.

That 1974 strike remains the reference point. According to Wikipedia it ran from 8 to 27 May 1974 and involved about 1.7 million workers, roughly seventy per cent of the permanent railway workforce. It was led by George Fernandes, then President of the All India Railwaymen's Federation (AIRF). The causes included stagnant pay scales and the long hours of locomotive staff, whose work the Railways treated as continuous, so that the eight-hour day was never applied to them. The Government suppressed the strike firmly. The AIRF's own account, which dates the start to 2 May after Fernandes's arrest in Lucknow and its end to 28 May, says that about 50,000 workers were arrested and more than 10,300 were dismissed, and that employees were reinstated after a change of government. The two sources differ by a day or so on the dates, and any count of arrests comes from the union's side, but the scale of the event is not in doubt. The AIRF also says that the productivity-linked bonus introduced in 1977-78 was a result of the strike.

The lesson that many railway unions drew from it, whether they supported the strike or not, was that this is a workforce whose collective action carries national consequences, and that the machinery for talking, from departmental councils to the Railway Board, matters enormously.

## How recognition works

Recognition on the railways is not a formality. It decides which federations sit in departmental councils, receive official facilities and are consulted by the Railway Board. It is awarded after **secret ballot elections** among employees.

The most recent round took place from **4 to 6 December 2024**, across 17 railway zones and two production units, the Chittaranjan Locomotive Works and the Rail Coach Factory at Kapurthala, according to a report in People's Democracy. The same report says a federation has to win recognition in at least six railways and 15 per cent of the valid votes polled across the system. The Railway Board then granted recognition for five years, by a letter dated 13 January 2025, to two federations, the AIRF and the National Federation of Indian Railwaymen (NFIR). Business Standard reported that each had cleared the 15 per cent mark.

BRMS came third. ThePrint reported that it won **10.12 per cent** of the votes across zonal railways and production units, short of the 15 per cent needed. A Railway Board letter dated 16 January 2025 nevertheless gave it certain facilities: informal meetings with senior officers, office accommodation in railway premises, and special invitee status at meetings at Board level. It did not carry the privileges that full recognition brings, such as special casual leave and passes for office bearers. Other unions asked for similar parity, which gives some idea of how closely these facilities are watched.

Recognition also comes with conditions. According to the Business Standard report, recognised federations must follow the Indian Railway Establishment Manual, may not keep a political fund, and may have as office bearers only serving or honourably retired railway employees. Recognition can be withdrawn or suspended if the conditions are broken.

For a federation like BRMS, the numbers have a plain meaning. Ten per cent of the votes is a significant base, and the gap to the threshold is about five percentage points. Closing it requires winning in more zones, and in zones with large workforces. In the Southern Railway, for example, People's Democracy reports that the BRMS affiliate won around 4 per cent of the vote in an electorate of 76,653, while the leading unions were each above a third. That kind of unevenness is where the work of an organising federation lies.

## What the workforce looks like

The railways have hired heavily in recent years. In a written reply to the Rajya Sabha on 5 December 2025, the Government said that 5.08 lakh people were recruited between 2014-15 and 2024-25, against 4.11 lakh in the previous decade, and that recruitment against 1,20,579 vacancies was taken up under the annual calendars for 2024 and 2025. These are Government figures, and they say little about how many posts remain vacant in the safety category, which is a separate matter that unions keep raising.

## Issues railway unions regularly raise

- **Pension.** The old pension scheme was replaced for new central government recruits by the National Pension System from 1 January 2004, and railway staff recruited after that date are covered. The Unified Pension Scheme approved by the Cabinet on 24 August 2024, and effective from 1 April 2025, offers an assured pension of 50 per cent of average basic pay over the last twelve months for those with at least 25 years of service, a minimum of Rs 10,000 a month after ten years, and a family pension of 60 per cent. Unions have debated whether this goes far enough.
- **Vacancies.** Empty posts in safety categories mean heavier duty on the remaining staff.
- **Running staff.** Duty hours and rest for loco pilots, guards and others whose work is round the clock, which was also a cause of the 1974 strike.
- **Outsourcing and corporatisation.** Opposition to the privatisation of production units and services.
- **Pay commission recommendations and allowances.**

## BMS's position

BMS's general position, reflected in the railway federation's work, is that the railways are a public asset and a public service, and that policy changes should be made after consultation with the workforce. It argues for filling vacancies, for rest and safe working hours for running staff, and for pension security. BRMS pursues these through its participation in the ballots, through representations to the Railway Board and through the facilities it has now been given.

## What remains to be done

Three tasks stand out. The first is organisational: to improve BRMS's vote share zone by zone before the next secret ballot. The second is to see whether the formal arrangements for non-recognised federations are enough for effective representation. The third is substantive: to keep the questions of safety staffing and duty hours in front of the Board and the public. As the 1974 strike showed, when the railway worker is ignored the cost is shared by everyone who relies on the trains.
